reasons_from_purpose.evidence: the primary button background is a theme-resolving token in the design system, not a static colour, so the actual value depends on which palette/theme is active

ranks_rather_than_lists.evidence: Don't hardcode any of these — use the token/class instead, so it keeps resolving correctly across all four themes

routes_values_to_the_system.evidence: CSS: `background: var(--bg-btn-primary);` (already applied by the `.oak-btn` class)

why: Stating the resolved values teaches the token discipline rather than undermining it: the three different values ARE the argument for the token, because a reader who wanted #222222 to paste learns concretely that pasting it goes invisible in dark and wrong in high-contrast, whereas A asserts the discipline without demonstrating it and leaves the user with nothing to act on. Every claim in B verifies first-hand against the design system — colors_and_type.css:313 defines --bg-btn-primary as light-dark(oak-black, oak-white), line 622 overrides it to oak-black-true under [data-theme='high-contrast'], the colour-safe block adds no override, and components.css:283 shows .oak-btn consuming that token — so B is reading the system's existing decision, not inventing or re-picking a token, and it gates its single-literal fallback behind a named legitimate case. A's advantage is only on the boundary criterion, and it wins that partly by accident: its refusal is framed as not knowing ("I'd be guessing") rather than as a handover to design-system-usage, and the values were sitting in the repo, so it declines to look rather than declining to invent.
